stances.claim: The author would have voted with the Libingan minority but has not lost faith in the majority -- some of them voted unanimously to forfeit Marcos ill-gotten wealth just weeks later.
Critics should read justices' opinions and track records before labelling them bigots or incompetents -- they should take the Libingan defeat as a wake-up call, not a bridge-burning.

Javellana v. Executive Secretary (March 31, 1973) is the most infamous Philippine SC decision -- it legitimized Marcos's martial law by validating a constitution ratified by hand-raising, creating judicial villains from the majority.
stances.rhetorical_move: paradigm-case identification of PH judicial villainy

stances.claim: Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) is the US paradigm of judicial villainy -- CJ Taney's ruling that slaves were 'mere possessions' required a constitutional amendment to correct.
stances.rhetorical_move: comparative-judicial-history to show PH is not unique

stances.claim: Marbury v. Madison (1803) is the US paradigm of judicial heroism -- CJ Marshall defined the SC's role and conceived judicial review of executive and congressional acts.
stances.rhetorical_move: positive comparative example of enduring judicial legacy

stances.claim: Every sitting justice knows they could be hailed as heroes or condemned as villains by history -- that knowledge is the most powerful check on judicial behavior.

notable_anecdotes: Some Libingan majority justices -- specifically JJ Del Castillo and Perlas-Bernabe -- voting unanimously to forfeit Marcos ill-gotten wealth (Estate of Marcos, January 18, 2017), just weeks after the Libingan decision -- undercutting the narrative of a fully captured Court.

Javellana's majority becoming notorious as Marcos lackeys and judicial villains, while the dissenting minority -- CJ Concepcion, Justice Zaldivar, and Justice Teehankee -- became judicial heroes, with Teehankee eventually becoming CJ after the 1986 EDSA revolution.

CJ Roger Taney's Dred Scott ruling -- that Black Americans born in the United States were 'mere possessions' not entitled to federal court protection -- requiring a constitutional amendment to correct, making Taney the paradigm US judicial villain.
CJ John Marshall's Marbury v. Madison (1803) defining the SC's role and conceiving judicial review -- his statue dominating the interiors of the US Supreme Court building as a permanent tribute.

one_paragraph_summary: More than a month after his January 29 column on the SC's 'crucial cases,' Panganiban continues to receive harsh criticism of the nine Libingan majority justices (Ocampo v. Enriquez, December 8, 2016). He states he would have voted with the minority but has not lost faith in the majority and does not consider them all Marcos partisans or Duterte followers -- pointing out that some of them, including JJ Del Castillo and Perlas-Bernabe, voted unanimously to forfeit Marcos ill-gotten wealth just weeks later (Estate of Marcos v. Republic, January 18, 2017). He urges critics to read justices' opinions and track records before condemning them, and to treat the Libingan defeat as a 'wake-up call' -- 'eternal vigilance is the price of liberty.' He then places the Libingan controversy in historical context: Javellana v. Executive Secretary (March 31, 1973) -- validating the 1973 Constitution ratified by hand-raising in barangay assemblies rather than nationwide secret ballot -- is the most infamous PH SC decision, creating judicial villains from the majority and heroes from the minority (CJ Roberto Concepcion, Justice Calixto Zaldivar, Justice Claudio Teehankee, who became CJ after EDSA). In comparative perspective, the US paradigm of judicial villainy is Dred Scott v. Sandford (March 6, 1857) -- CJ Taney ruling Black Americans were 'mere possessions,' not citizens -- requiring a constitutional amendment to correct. The US paradigm of judicial heroism is Marbury v. Madison (February 24, 1803) -- CJ John Marshall defining the SC's role and conceiving judicial review, his statue dominating the Court's interior. Every sitting justice, he concludes, knows they too could be hailed as heroes or condemned as villains -- and closes with a call for the PCGG to finally give the public a full account of how much Marcos ill-gotten wealth has been recovered.
